## References

1. [Tulu 3: Pushing Frontiers in Open Language Model Post-Training (RLVR)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.15124)

# Notes

## The problem this paper exists to solve

By late 2024 there was a wide and growing gap between **open-weight base models** (Llama 3.1, Qwen 2.5, OLMo) and the **post-training recipes** that turn a raw next-token predictor into a useful assistant. Base models are released openly, but the *post-training* — the SFT data, the preference data, the RL stage, the eval suite, the decontamination process — is where almost all the proprietary value lives, and it is almost universally hidden. Even "open" instruct models (Llama 3.1 Instruct, Qwen 2.5 Instruct) ship only the final weights: you cannot see the data, you cannot reproduce the recipe, and you cannot learn *why* it works.

Tülu 3, from Ai2 (Allen Institute for AI), is an attempt to close that gap end-to-end. It is not a new architecture — it post-trains Llama 3.1 8B and 70B base models (and later 405B) — but it releases **everything**: model weights at every stage (SFT, DPO, final), the full training code (`open-instruct`), the eval framework (`olmes`), the decontamination tooling, and crucially **all the datasets** including the synthetic ones. The headline empirical claim: the resulting models beat the official instruct versions of Llama 3.1, Qwen 2.5, and Mistral at matched size, and at 70B the model surpasses GPT-3.5-Turbo and GPT-4o-mini and approaches Claude 3.5 Haiku — while being fully reproducible.

The standout *methodological* contribution is the final training stage: **RLVR — Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards**. This is the idea that became one of the most important threads in the field (it is the same family of technique that DeepSeek-R1 and the reasoning-model wave later scaled up).

## The core idea, simply

A standard RLHF pipeline trains a **reward model (RM)** — a learned neural net that scores how "good" a response is — and then uses PPO to push the policy toward high-RM responses. The reward model is the weak link: it is expensive to train, it drifts, and the policy learns to *hack* it (find responses that score high without actually being good).

RLVR's insight is dead simple: **for tasks where you can mechanically check whether the answer is correct, throw the learned reward model away and use the checker as the reward.** If the model solves a math problem and the final answer matches the gold answer, give it reward. If it follows a verifiable instruction ("respond in exactly 3 bullet points, all lowercase"), check the constraint programmatically and reward it. The reward is *grounded in ground truth*, so it cannot be hacked the way a learned RM can.

That is the whole conceptual move. The rest of the paper is (a) the *full* pipeline that makes a frontier-quality model around this idea, and (b) the careful data + eval engineering that makes the result reproducible and trustworthy.

## The four-stage recipe (data flow)

Tülu 3 is built as a deliberate **pipeline**, each stage consuming the output of the last:

**Stage 0 — Prompt curation & synthesis.** They first define the *target skills*: knowledge recall, reasoning, math, coding, precise instruction following, safety, multilinguality, general chat. Then they assemble prompts from public datasets **and** generate large amounts of **synthetic data** to fill gaps. The synthetic-data engine is **persona-driven**: they take ~250K personas from Persona Hub (e.g. "A machine learning researcher focused on neural networks"), and feed a persona + a synthesis prompt to GPT-4o to steer it into generating diverse, skill-targeted instructions and responses. For precise instruction following they seed with ~33 verifiable instruction *types* and generate ~30K verifiable instruction–response pairs (IF-PERSONA-SFT); for math/code they generate ~220K and ~35K instances respectively. Persona-conditioning is the trick that buys *diversity* — without it, an LLM asked to "generate a math problem" collapses to the same handful of templates.

**Stage 1 — Supervised Finetuning (SFT).** Standard next-token cross-entropy on the curated + synthetic prompt-completion mixture (`tulu-3-sft-mixture`). The mixture is *tuned* per-skill: they run ablations adding/removing each skill's data and watch the eval suite, balancing so that improving math doesn't regress safety, etc. Output: `Llama-3.1-Tulu-3-{8B,70B}-SFT`.

**Stage 2 — Preference tuning via length-normalized DPO.** They build a large **preference dataset** and optimize with DPO. Two design choices matter:
- *On-policy preference data.* For each prompt they sample completions from a **pool of models** *including the Tülu-3 SFT model itself*, then use **GPT-4o as an LLM judge** (rating multiple aspects, UltraFeedback-style) to label which completion is chosen vs rejected. They show that *including on-policy completions* (responses from their own SFT model, not just off-policy outputs from other models) measurably improves downstream DPO. Intuition: the preference signal is most useful where it lives near the policy's actual output distribution. They validated that GPT-4o, GPT-4-turbo, and Llama-3.1-405B agree closely as judges; GPT-4o was chosen for cost/throughput.
- *Length-normalized DPO.* They compared DPO, SimPO, and PPO and found **length-normalized DPO** gave the best performance with the least complexity, so they "prioritized simplicity and efficiency." Output: `Llama-3.1-Tulu-3-{8B,70B}-DPO`.

**Stage 3 — RLVR.** The novel RL stage, applied on top of the DPO checkpoint, targeting the verifiable skills (GSM8K, MATH, IFEval). This is where the contribution lives.

## DPO, symbol by symbol

Vanilla DPO replaces the RM-then-PPO loop with a direct closed-form loss on preference pairs. Given a prompt `x`, a chosen response `y_w`, and a rejected response `y_l`, with policy `π_θ` and frozen reference `π_ref` (the SFT model):

```
L_DPO = − log σ( β · [ log(π_θ(y_w|x)/π_ref(y_w|x)) − log(π_θ(y_l|x)/π_ref(y_l|x)) ] )
```

- `σ` is the logistic sigmoid; the bracket is the difference in *implicit reward* between chosen and rejected, where the implicit reward of a response is `β · log(π_θ/π_ref)`.
- `β` controls how far the policy may move from the reference. Maximizing this pushes the chosen log-prob up and the rejected log-prob down, *relative to the reference*.

The problem DPO has: the sum `log π_θ(y|x) = Σ_t log π_θ(y_t|...)` grows with response length, so the implicit reward is **length-biased** — DPO can exploit length rather than quality. **Length-normalized DPO** divides each log-probability by the response token count `|y|`, so the per-response signal is a *mean* log-prob rather than a sum:

```
implicit reward(y) ∝ (β / |y|) · log(π_θ(y|x)/π_ref(y|x))
```

This decouples preference learning from length and is what made DPO outperform SimPO/PPO in their runs. (For the broader PPO-vs-DPO-vs-GRPO landscape this sits in, see [[PPO vs GRPO - Policy Optimization for Alignment]].)

## RLVR, symbol by symbol

RLVR reuses the **standard RLHF/PPO objective** but swaps the learned reward model for a deterministic **verification function** `v(x, y)`. The objective being maximized over the policy `π_θ`:

```
max_θ  E_{y ~ π_θ(·|x)} [ R_RLVR(x, y) ]
       = E[ v(x, y) − β · KL( π_θ(y|x) ‖ π_ref(y|x) ) ]
```

Walking the symbols:
- `v(x, y)` is the **verifiable reward**. It returns a constant `α` (the paper uses **α = 10**) when the completion `y` is verified correct for prompt `x`, and **0** otherwise. This is a *binary, ground-truth* signal — there is nothing to reward-hack, because the only way to get reward is to actually be correct.
- The verifier is **task-specific**: for GSM8K/MATH it is exact-match on the extracted final answer against the gold answer (with answer-normalization); for IFEval it is the suite of programmatic constraint checks (length, casing, keyword presence, format) — the same checks IFEval uses for evaluation, now used as the training signal.
- `β · KL(π_θ ‖ π_ref)` is the usual KL penalty anchoring the policy to the reference (the DPO checkpoint) so it doesn't collapse or drift off-distribution while chasing reward. `β` is the KL coefficient.
- Optimization is **PPO**. Reward is sparse (one scalar at the end of a completion, since correctness is only defined for the full answer), and they note an **asynchronous** setup using **vLLM** for fast generation decoupled from the optimizer.

**The value-model finding (a genuinely non-obvious design choice).** PPO needs a *value function* (critic) to estimate expected return for advantage computation. The intuitive choice is to initialize the value model from the policy/SFT model. Tülu 3 finds instead that **initializing the value function from a general reward model** yields the *highest* GSM8K test score and best average — "highlighting the importance of the value function." So even though RLVR discards the RM as the *reward signal*, the RM's learned representations are still valuable as a *critic initialization*. They also analyze the policy-init choice: starting RLVR from a *stronger* model (DPO) vs a *weaker* one (SFT) — both can reach the same level of verifiable reward, but the weaker start needs a *larger* KL budget, and starting stronger gives better test-set generalization. This is the kind of careful RL ablation usually missing from open recipes; for the underlying value-function / advantage machinery see [[Reinforcement Learning - Foundations, MDPs, and Control Algorithms]].

## What RLVR actually buys (the key numbers)

RLVR is the *last* stage, applied to an already-strong DPO model, so the gains are incremental but real and **targeted exactly at the verifiable skills**:

- **+3.3 points on GSM8K**, **+1.7 on MATH**, **+1.3 on IFEval** over the DPO checkpoint.

These are modest absolute numbers because the DPO model is already good — the point is that RLVR delivers *reliable, hack-free* improvement precisely where a ground-truth checker exists, without the reward-model overhead. The mechanism is exactly why this technique scaled so explosively afterwards: when you have a verifier, RL on verifiable reward is the cleanest possible signal, and you can pour as much compute into it as you want.

## Headline benchmark results

The flagship comparison is an **average over the full evaluation suite** (multi-task: MMLU, GSM8K, MATH, IFEval, HumanEval/coding, safety, knowledge, chat, etc.):

- **Tülu 3 70B ≈ 76.0 average**, surpassing **Llama 3.1 70B Instruct (~73.4)**, Qwen 2.5 72B Instruct, Hermes 3 70B, and Nemotron Llama 3.1 70B; it beats **GPT-3.5-Turbo** and **GPT-4o-mini**, and approaches **Claude 3.5 Haiku**.
- **Tülu 3 8B ≈ 60.4 average**, beating Llama 3.1 8B Instruct, Qwen 2.5 7B Instruct, and Ministral 8B at matched size.
- On **style-controlled ChatBot Arena**, Tülu 3 70B is roughly **tied with Llama 3.1 70B Instruct** — notable because it is the only model near that level with *fully open* post-training data and code.

(Exact per-task numbers shift slightly across paper revisions — v5 added fixed evals and 405B results — so treat the averages as the stable headline.)

## The evaluation framework — Tülu 3 Eval / OLMES

A subtle but important contribution: a **standardized eval suite split into a development set and an unseen/held-out set**. The dev benchmarks are used to *guide* recipe decisions (data mixing, hyperparameters) during the project; the unseen benchmarks are reserved to test whether improvements *generalize* rather than overfit to the eval targets. This split is what makes their claims credible — without a held-out set, iterating against your benchmarks is just slow overfitting.

This pairs with **aggressive decontamination**, made concrete: a test instance is considered contaminated if, using **8-gram** overlap, **>50% of its tokens** have 8-gram matches to a single training instance; and at the dataset level they drop any training source overlapping **>2%** of the eval suite. They release this tooling so others can audit and reuse it — directly attacking the credibility problem that "open" instruct models can't answer ("did you just train on the test set?").

## Non-obvious choices & honest limitations

- **RLVR only works where a verifier exists.** Math, formal instruction-following, and (later) code with unit tests are the natural fits. For open-ended chat, safety nuance, or "helpfulness," there *is* no ground-truth checker — those skills still rely on SFT + DPO with an LLM judge. RLVR is a sharp tool with a narrow blade, not a replacement for the whole pipeline.
- **Reward sparsity.** Because correctness is only defined for a complete answer, the reward is a single end-of-sequence scalar — credit assignment is hard, which is why the value-function init mattered so much.
- **Judge dependence.** The preference stage leans on GPT-4o as the labeler, so the model inherits whatever biases that judge has — a real (and acknowledged) form of distillation from a closed model inside an otherwise "fully open" recipe.
- **Incremental, not magical, RLVR gains** at this scale (single-digit point improvements). The *paradigm* turned out to matter far more than these specific deltas; Tülu 3 is best read as the careful, fully-documented introduction of verifiable-reward RL to open post-training, which the reasoning-model wave then scaled with GRPO-style optimizers and long chains of thought.

## Where this sits relative to prior & adjacent work

- **vs. RLHF (InstructGPT, Llama-2-chat):** same PPO machinery, but the learned reward model is replaced by a verifier for the subset of skills that admit one — eliminating reward hacking there.
- **vs. DPO-only recipes (Zephyr, Tülu 2):** Tülu 3 keeps DPO as a *stage* but adds the RLVR stage on top and pushes synthetic on-policy preference data much harder.
- **vs. closed instruct models:** the whole point — matched or better quality with full transparency.
- **Toward the reasoning era:** RLVR is the conceptual seed of the verifiable-reward RL that DeepSeek-R1 and o1-style models scaled; the policy-optimization choices it studies (PPO here, KL anchoring, value-init) are exactly the design space later contested by GRPO — see [[PPO vs GRPO - Policy Optimization for Alignment]] — over the RL foundations in [[Reinforcement Learning - Foundations, MDPs, and Control Algorithms]].

**One-line takeaway:** Tülu 3 is a fully-open, end-to-end post-training recipe whose key idea — RLVR, replacing the learned reward model with a ground-truth verifier (reward = α if correct, else 0, optimized with PPO under a KL penalty) — gives clean, unhackable RL signal on math/instruction-following, and which (with persona-driven synthetic data, on-policy length-normalized DPO, and a dev/unseen eval split with aggressive 8-gram decontamination) produces an 8B/70B model family that beats the open instruct baselines and rivals GPT-4o-mini / Claude 3.5 Haiku.
